content: The effectiveness of the contraceptive patch depends on the user’s adherence to the prescribed schedule. The risk of pregnancy is highest when a woman delays changing the patch. When used as commonly practiced, approximately 7 out of 100 women using the combined patch will become pregnant during the first year of use. This means that 93 out of 100 women will not become pregnant. If the patch is used perfectly, with no mistakes, the pregnancy rate is less than 1 per 100 women in the first year (3 per 1,000 women). Pregnancy rates may be slightly higher in women weighing 90 kg (198 lbs) or more. Fertility returns immediately after discontinuing the patch, with no delay. However, the patch does not provide protection against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The patch is considered safe and suitable for nearly all women, including those who have or have not had children, are married or unmarried, are of any age (including adolescents and women over 40), have given birth and are breastfeeding (after a certain period), have recently had an abortion, miscarriage, or ectopic pregnancy, smoke cigarettes (if under 35 years old), have anemia (current or past), have varicose veins, or are living with HIV (regardless of antiretroviral therapy use). To use the patch, the user should remove it from its pouch by tearing the foil along the edge, then peel away the backing without touching the sticky surface. The patch can be applied to clean, dry skin on the upper outer arm, back, stomach, abdomen, or buttocks, but not on the breasts. The sticky, medicated part should be pressed against the skin for 10 seconds, and the edges should be smoothed to ensure it adheres properly. The patch remains secure during activities such as work, exercise, swimming, and bathing. It must be changed weekly for three consecutive weeks, with each new patch applied on the same day of the week (e.g., if the first patch is applied on a Sunday, all subsequent patches should also be applied on Sundays). To avoid skin irritation, the new patch should not be applied to the same spot as the previous one. No patch is worn during the fourth week, during which monthly bleeding typically occurs. After the patch-free week, a new patch should be applied. The user should never go more than seven days without wearing a patch, as this increases the risk of pregnancy. Some users report side effects such as skin irritation or rash at the application site, changes in bleeding patterns (e.g., lighter bleeding, fewer days of bleeding, irregular bleeding, prolonged bleeding, or no monthly bleeding), headaches, nausea, vomiting, breast tenderness or pain, abdominal pain, flu-like symptoms or upper respiratory infections, and vaginal irritation, redness, or inflammation (vaginitis). Long-term studies on the patch are limited, but researchers expect its health benefits and risks to be similar to those of combined oral contraceptives (COCs). The known health benefits of the patch include protection against pregnancy, endometrial cancer, ovarian cancer, and symptomatic pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). It may also help protect against ovarian cysts and iron-deficiency anemia. Additionally, it reduces menstrual cramps, menstrual bleeding problems, ovulation pain, excess hair on the face or body, symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (e.g., irregular bleeding, acne, excess hair), and symptoms of endometriosis (e.g., pelvic pain, irregular bleeding). Known health risks of COCs, which may also apply to the patch, include very rare occurrences of blood clots in the deep veins of the legs or lungs (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) and extremely rare occurrences of stroke or heart attack. The combined contraceptive vaginal ring (CVR), also known as the NuvaRing, is a flexible ring that a woman places in her vagina. It continuously releases two hormones, a progestin and an estrogen, similar to the natural hormones progesterone and estrogen in a woman’s body. These hormones are absorbed through the vaginal wall directly into the bloodstream. The ring is left in place for three weeks and removed during the fourth week, during which monthly bleeding occurs. The CVR primarily works by preventing ovulation. Its effectiveness depends on proper use, with the risk of pregnancy being highest when a woman is late in starting a new ring. When used as commonly practiced, about 7 out of 100 women using the CVR will become pregnant in the first year, meaning 93 out of 100 women will not become pregnant. With perfect use, the pregnancy rate is less than 1 per 100 women in the first year (3 per 1,000 women). Fertility returns immediately after discontinuing the ring, with no delay. The CVR does not provide protection against STIs. To use the CVR, the user can choose a comfortable position (e.g., standing with one leg up, squatting, or lying down). She should press opposite sides of the ring together and gently push the folded ring entirely inside the vagina. The exact position is not important, but inserting it deeply helps it stay in place and reduces the likelihood of feeling it. The vaginal muscles naturally keep the ring in place. The ring must remain in place at all times, day and night, for three weeks. At the end of the third week, the user can remove the ring and dispose of it in a waste receptacle (not a flush toilet). The ring should be removed for the fourth week, during which monthly bleeding typically occurs. If the ring is left in for up to a fourth week, no special action is needed. However, the ring should never be left out for more than 48 hours until the fourth week. If the ring slips out, it should be rinsed in clean water and reinserted immediately. The ring can be removed for sex or cleaning, but this is not necessary and is not recommended, as some women forget to put it back within 48 hours. Side effects reported by CVR users include changes in bleeding patterns (e.g., lighter bleeding, fewer days of bleeding, irregular bleeding, infrequent bleeding, or no monthly bleeding), headaches, dizziness, nausea, breast tenderness, weight changes, mood changes, acne (which can improve or worsen but usually improves), and other physical changes such as slight increases in blood pressure. Blood pressure typically returns to normal after discontinuing use. The CVR shares the same health benefits and risks as COCs. The progesterone-releasing vaginal ring (PVR) is a smooth, soft, flexible silicone ring placed in the vagina to prolong lactational amenorrhea (delaying the return of monthly bleeding) and help breastfeeding women space pregnancies. It continuously releases natural progesterone, similar to that in a woman’s body, directly into the bloodstream through the vaginal wall. The PVR does not contain estrogen. It is used starting 4–9 weeks after giving birth, with each ring kept in place for 90 days. The user can replace it with a new ring immediately, using up to four rings consecutively without breaks. The PVR works by preventing ovulation and extending postpartum amenorrhea in breastfeeding women. It is a safe and effective option for women who have a baby at least four weeks old, are breastfeeding at least four times per day, and whose monthly bleeding has not returned. The PVR is highly effective, with 1–2 pregnancies per 100 women using it for a year. Fertility returns immediately after discontinuing use, with no delay. The PVR does not provide protection against STIs. It is suitable for postpartum women who are actively breastfeeding at least four times per day. The ring must remain in place at all times to maintain effectiveness. It can be removed for sex or cleaning, but this is not necessary and is not recommended, as some women forget to put it back within two hours. If the ring slips out, it should be rinsed in clean water and reinserted immediately. The partner may feel the ring during intercourse, but this generally does not interfere with sexual activity or pleasure. Side effects reported by PVR users include spotting or irregular bleeding, low-abdominal pain, breast pain, and vaginal discharge. The PVR does not affect breast milk production or composition and supports continued breastfeeding and healthy infant nutrition. It is safe and effective based on several one-year studies, with health risks similar to those of progestin-only pills.
